author: Baron Godfrey Rathbone Benson Charnwood
claims: Lincoln's handling of the emergency threatening his Government threw into shade the weakness he had hitherto shown.
Preparations were made for possible expeditions to Fort Sumter and Fort Pickens.
Seward caused trouble through officious interference regarding these preparations.
An announcement was sent to the Governor of South Carolina that provisions would be sent to Fort Sumter, with assurances that no further steps would be taken if unopposed.
The eventual decision to send provisions but not troops to Fort Sumter was Lincoln's decision.
This decision was not made until Senators and Congressmen made it clear that Northern opinion would support him.
The decision was the right one as it avoided the appearance of provocation while upholding the Union's right.
The decision was taken perilously late, risking the Government's humiliation.
Jefferson Davis was urged by an Alabama gentleman to not delay the impending struggle, with the assertion that Alabama would return to the Union if blood was not shed.
Buchanan was informed that troops and ships of war should be sent if the Union Government desired to hold the Charleston forts.
Congressmen from South Carolina claimed the forts on their soil as their own and sought assurances that they would not be reinforced.
Buchanan refused to promise not to reinforce the forts but also refused entreaties to reinforce them, fearing it would precipitate conflict.
Major Anderson withdrew his force to Fort Sumter due to insufficient men to hold all forts if attacked.
The Governor of South Carolina protested Anderson's withdrawal as a violation of an understanding with the President and seized the arsenal and custom house.
Commissioners from South Carolina requested the surrender of the forts, offering payment for property.
Seward was loyal to Lincoln and informed him of his actions, and was candid with Campbell and his friends about his lack of authority.
Seward spoke freely and rashly of his hopes.
Lincoln cautioned Seward and gave him freedom, but may have told Douglas he intended to evacuate Fort Sumter.
The Government's decision was delayed by negotiations that were known to be futile.
The Southern Government and Commissioners felt deceived by these negotiations.
Seward sent Lincoln a paper titled "Some Thoughts for the President's Consideration" on April 1, criticizing the lack of policy and proposing a foreign policy to end domestic dissensions.
Lincoln reserved his judgment on the Fort Sumter situation until the question nearly settled itself to his disgrace.
Lincoln lacked rough perception and vigor, unlike Jackson.
Lincoln had declared he would take no provocative step.
The risk of overruling his Cabinet's opinion based on military advice was a lesser risk than the delay.
Lincoln's strength and weakness were shown in his not yielding to advisers and weighing the matter undisturbed by delay.
He decided only when sure of the political results.
Commissioners from the Southern Confederacy sought interviews with Seward to treat for recognition and peaceful surrender of forts.
Virginia's action was in the balance, and a "Peace Convention" was summoned by Virginia.
